Multi-year digital accessibility plan in France: annotated template, action plan, KPIs

Published on 12 November 2026Reading time: 29 minutesBy the firm’s team

SPANArticle 47(III), French law of 11 February 2005
3 years maximum, one action plan per year

The multi-year digital accessibility plan, known in French law as the schéma pluriannuel de mise en accessibilité and often abbreviated to SPAN, is the document in which a French public body or a large company sets out, for a maximum of three years, its digital accessibility policy and its timetable for bringing its services into compliance. A search for the term mostly returns dozens of PDFs published by organisations, of very uneven quality, with no explanation of what is required or of what the regulator actually checks. This guide starts from the text of the law and the official RGAA page, then provides a section-by-section annotated template, an example of an annual action plan, monitoring indicators and the list of errors that expose an organisation to formal notice from Arcom, the French regulator.

The multi-year accessibility plan: a management tool, not a statement of good intentions

The multi-year plan is the third transparency document required by French law, alongside the accessibility statement (déclaration d’accessibilité) and the compliance notice displayed on the home page. The statement says where a given service stands on a given date; the multi-year plan says how the organisation intends to improve, with what resources, what organisation and what timetable. The annual action plan (plan d’actions annuel) is its operational translation for the current year.

In practice, many published plans look alike: a page of general commitment, a list of good intentions (“raise staff awareness”, “audit our websites”), rarely a budget, and almost never a deadline or a named owner. A document of this kind ticks a box on paper, but it is of no use internally and does not hold up well under inspection, because Arcom checks that the plan is present and that it complies, not merely that it exists. A good plan, by contrast, tells senior management what will be fixed, when, by whom and at what cost.

Nor is the multi-year plan an audit report. It relies on existing audits, but its subject is the organisation: who owns the topic, how accessibility is built into projects, purchasing, recruitment and training, and how known defects will be dealt with. That is what distinguishes it from the accessibility statement, which focuses on one specific service, and what makes it the management tool for the whole approach described in our guide to digital accessibility. For an international group used to accessibility policies written at headquarters, the French plan is closer to a dated, published compliance programme than to a policy document.

Key point

Three documents go together: the statement (the status of one service), the multi-year plan (the policy and timetable over a maximum of three years) and the action plan for the current year (the dated work). Each must refer to the others, and all three must be kept up to date.

What French law says about the multi-year plan, word for word

The obligation is set out in paragraph III of article 47 of Law No. 2005-102 of 11 February 2005, as amended by Ordinance No. 2023-859 of 6 September 2023: the persons listed in paragraph I “publient une déclaration d’accessibilité et élaborent un schéma pluriannuel de mise en accessibilité de leurs services de communication au public en ligne, qui est rendu public et décliné en plans d’actions annuels, et dont la durée ne peut être supérieure à trois ans” (“publish an accessibility statement and draw up a multi-year plan for making their online public communication services accessible, which is made public and broken down into annual action plans, and whose duration may not exceed three years”). The text can be read in the current version of article 47 on Légifrance (in French).

Four requirements follow directly from this sentence. The plan covers all of the organisation’s online public communication services: websites, intranets, extranets, mobile apps, software packages and digital street furniture. It is made public. It lasts three years at most. It is broken down into annual action plans. Paragraph IV of the same article adds that every service gives “aisément et directement accès” (“easy and direct access”) to the statement, the multi-year plan and the action plan for the current year.

The decree of 24 July 2019 and the RGAA

Decree No. 2019-768 of 24 July 2019 supplements the law on three points that matter for the plan. Its article 5 leaves it to the framework, the RGAA (Référentiel général d’amélioration de l’accessibilité, France’s General Accessibility Improvement Framework), to set the format and the information that the documents provided for in article 47(III) must contain, that is, the statement, the multi-year plan and the annual plans. Its article 6 requires the statement to include a link to the multi-year plan. Its article 7 requires the continuing training of staff who work on online services to include theoretical and practical instruction in digital accessibility: the multi-year plan is the natural place to schedule that training.

Decree No. 2026-816 of 24 August 2026 amended the 2019 text, notably its article 5, and repealed the former article 8 on penalties, but it changed neither the mandatory link to the multi-year plan in the statement nor the training obligation. The expected content of the plan is set out, heading by heading, on the official RGAA page on the multi-year plan (in French), which we follow in the next section.

Who is covered

All the organisations listed in article 47(I) must draw up a multi-year plan: the State, local and regional authorities and their public institutions, other legal persons governed by public law, private legal persons entrusted with a public service mission, those created to meet needs in the general interest whose activity is mainly financed by public bodies or whose management is subject to their control, and companies whose turnover generated in France exceeds €250 million. Under article 2 of the 2019 decree, that threshold is calculated for each legal person, on the basis of the average annual turnover generated in France over the last three financial years closed before the year in question. The details of the scope and of the threshold calculation are set out in our article on digital accessibility obligations in France.

Companies subject to the European Accessibility Act solely through the French Consumer Code, without exceeding the article 47 threshold, do not have to publish a multi-year plan: their obligations are of a different kind, as our article on the European Accessibility Act explains. Nothing prevents a mid-sized company from adopting a voluntary plan, however: it is often the simplest way to organise EAA compliance.

Enforcement and penalties

Since the 2023 ordinance, article 47-1 of the 2005 law (in French) has given enforcement powers to Arcom (Autorité de régulation de la communication audiovisuelle et numérique, the French regulator for audiovisual and digital communication). The authority has failings recorded in an official report, serves formal notice on the organisation to comply within a time limit it sets, and makes that formal notice public. If the organisation does not comply, it may impose a financial penalty, together with publication of the penalty where appropriate. The ceiling is €50,000 for failing to meet the accessibility requirements and €25,000 for the obligations in paragraphs III and IV, which include the multi-year plan and the annual plan. Where the same failing persists six months after a penalty, a new penalty may be imposed.

For companies above the threshold, Arcom’s powers cover only those obligations in paragraphs III and IV: the statement, the multi-year plan, the action plan, the home page notice and access to these documents. In other words, for a large company, the multi-year plan and the action plan are precisely what the regulator can penalise. Arcom’s English-language page on the accessibility of digital sites and services says so clearly: the authority checks the presence and conformity of the accessibility statement, of the organisation’s multi-year accessibility plan and of the action plan for the current year.

The mandatory content of the multi-year accessibility plan, heading by heading

The official RGAA page describes two blocks. The first presents the organisation’s policy: strategy, accessibility lead, resources, skills, training, organisation and purchasing. The second presents the compliance work: new projects, user testing, audits, corrective measures and timetable, non-mandatory measures and a review of the annual plans. The table below takes each heading, explains what should actually be written under it and the evidence that makes it credible.

Expected content of a French multi-year digital accessibility plan under the RGAA, and what to write
Heading required by the RGAAWhat to write in practiceEvidence or verifiable elementCommon error
Accessibility in the digital strategy and disability policyThe link with the digital master plan, the disability or CSR policy, and the body that approves the planReference and date of the approval decisionGeneral commitment not attached to any governing body
Position and duties of the accessibility leadJob title, reporting line, share of working time, duties, any power to block a release at acceptance stageJob description, letter of appointmentLead named with no dedicated time and no reporting line
Human and financial resourcesInternal full-time equivalents, annual budget per item (audits, fixes, training, tools), source of fundingIdentified budget lineNo figure at all, or “appropriate resources”
Skills in job descriptions and recruitmentRoles concerned (development, design, content, purchasing), standard wording for job descriptionsExtract from a job descriptionHeading forgotten
Training and awarenessLearning paths by role, volume, priority audiences, timetableTraining plan, number of people trained“Raise staff awareness” with no audience or volume
External resources and expertise, toolsUse of specialist auditors or developers, testing tools, acceptance test environmentsCurrent contracts or public procurement contractsList of automated tools presented as an audit method
Internal organisation and handling of requestsApproval process, checks on services before going live, handling of user reports and response timeWritten procedure, register of requestsContact address that nobody monitors
Contract clauses and acceptance testingRequirements in specifications and quotes, award criterion, acceptance procedure, agreements with partnersStandard clause, scoring gridAccessibility absent from redesign contracts
New projectsAccessibility required from the design stage, checkpointsCheckpoints in the project methodAudit only after the service goes live
Testing with disabled peopleProjects concerned, frequency, user profilesTest reportsEmpty heading
Planned compliance assessmentsList of services, date of the last audit, date of the next oneAudit scheduleOnly the main websites are listed
Corrective measures and timetableKnown defects, priority given to the most visited content, deadlinesLink to the audit reportsTimetable with no dates

Two points of method. First, the official page does not impose strict headings for the multi-year plan, unlike the format of the statement, where Arcom noted renamed or missing sections in its formal notice of June 2026. Following the order and wording of the RGAA is nonetheless the safest way to show that no heading has been left out. Second, the RGAA does not specify which body adopts the plan. Explicit approval by the chief executive, the executive committee or, for a local authority, its executive gives the document a weight that a simple upload by the communications department does not.

For a group whose working language is English, a practical question arises: in which language should the plan be published? The French texts do not address it explicitly in the pages cited here, but the plan is meant for users of French services and for French inspectors. Publishing it in French, using the RGAA headings, avoids any debate; an English version can be added for internal governance, provided both versions say the same thing.

Multi-year plan, annual action plan and statement: how to align them without contradiction

The three documents answer one another, and Arcom reads them together. A non-compliance listed in a service’s statement must be matched by a fix in an action plan; an exemption claimed on grounds of disproportionate burden must be reconsidered when the plan is revised; an audit announced in the plan must lead to an updated statement. The RGAA specifies that the multi-year plan and the plan for the current year are available online on the organisation’s website, published in an accessible format, and that the statement contains links to them.

The timetable is the most common weak point. A multi-year plan covers three years at most, but nothing requires it to follow the calendar year, nor to wait until it expires before revising it. The action plan, however, covers “l’année en cours” (“the current year”): from 1 January, the previous year’s plan no longer meets the obligation. This is exactly the failing found on impots.gouv.fr, the French tax administration’s website, in Arcom’s decision of 24 June 2026, available in English: the official report of 30 April 2026 found that the published action plan covered 2024, which constitutes a breach of article 47(IV). The authority allowed two months to remedy it.

Example timetable for a 2027-2029 multi-year accessibility plan
PeriodDocument to publish or updateKey contentLink with the statement
October-December 20262027-2029 multi-year plan approved, 2027 action planPolicy, resources, timetable for audits and fixesLink to the new plan added to every statement
1 January 20272027 plan published, 2026 plan removed from the main pageDated actions for the year“2027 action plan” link
January 20282028 action plan with a review of the 2027 planPostponed actions, new actionsStatements of re-audited services updated
January 20292029 action plan with a review of 2028Preparation of the next multi-year planCheck that every statement is still valid
End of 2029 at the latest2030-2032 multi-year planReview of the three annual plansLink to the new plan

Keep the plans of previous years in an “Archives” section of the accessibility page, separate from the link to the current plan: they are the evidence for the review required by the RGAA. The main link, however, the one given in the statement and the one a sworn inspector will follow, must point to the plan for the current year, without any ambiguity.

Before writing: the initial assessment in six weeks

A credible plan is not written from a template found online. It is written from an inventory of what the organisation publishes, what it knows about its level of compliance and what it buys. For a medium-sized local authority or a company division, six weeks is generally enough to gather the information, provided a project lead is appointed from the outset.

  1. Weeks 1 and 2: list the services. List every website, subdomain, intranet, extranet, mobile app, browser-based software package and booking or payment service bought from a software vendor. For each, note the owner, the supplier, the tool, the estimated audience and the date of the last redesign. Forgotten services are the leading cause of an incomplete plan.
  2. Week 2: gather existing audits and statements. For each service, find the date and rate of the last audit, the status shown on the home page and the date of the statement. A service without a valid audit must be declared non-compliant and given priority in the audit schedule. Our article on how an RGAA audit works helps you anticipate the time required.
  3. Week 3: list contracts and procurement. Record the contracts for development, third-party maintenance and content hosting, and the subscriptions to online software, with their expiry dates. Every renewal is an opportunity to introduce an accessibility requirement and an acceptance procedure.
  4. Week 4: map skills. Who, internally, knows how to fix a form, produce an accessible PDF, write a text alternative or audit a page? This map sets the training plan and the need for outside expertise.
  5. Week 5: collect user reports. Use the accessibility contact mailbox, complaints sent to customer service or the front desk, and feedback from disability organisations. They often reveal the most serious barriers, the ones a compliance rate does not show.
  6. Week 6: estimate costs and prioritise. Cross-reference the audience of each service, the nature of the procedures (payment, registration, applications for assistance) and the extent of known defects. The result is the ordered list that will feed the plan’s timetable and the first annual plan.

If most services have never been audited, the initial assessment naturally leads to a first wave of audits, included in the plan for year one. An RGAA audit of the priority services then gives the multi-year plan what it most often lacks: a measured baseline from which progress can be tracked.

In an international group, the inventory often turns up services that nobody in France thinks of as French: a careers portal run from headquarters, a customer area hosted by a regional shared service centre, an app published under the global brand. If the French entity subject to article 47 offers these services to the public in France, the question of whether they fall within its plan has to be settled explicitly, rather than discovered during an inspection.

Annotated template for a multi-year digital accessibility plan

The template below follows the order of the official RGAA page. Passages in square brackets are to be replaced; the comments explain what is expected of each part. It suits a public body as well as a company subject to article 47, with a few adaptations noted along the way. The sample wording is given in English; in the published French version, keep the RGAA terminology.

1. Preamble and scope

Sample text: “This multi-year digital accessibility plan of [organisation] covers the period from [1 January 2027] to [31 December 2029]. It was approved by [body] on [date]. It applies to the online public communication services listed in the appendix, namely [number] websites, [number] mobile apps and [number] software packages. It is broken down each year into an action plan published on the accessibility page of [website address].” Comment: the list of services in the appendix is essential; it is what makes it possible to check that each service has its statement and appears in the audit schedule.

2. Digital accessibility policy

Sample text: “Digital accessibility is part of [the digital master plan / the disability policy / the CSR strategy] of [organisation]. It applies to every new digital project and to every major change to an existing service.” Comment: cite the strategic document the plan is attached to and, for a public body, its link with the policy on employing disabled people. Avoid statements of intent with no operational consequence.

3. Digital accessibility lead

Sample text: “The digital accessibility lead is [job title], reporting to [department]. They devote [share of working time] to this role. They are responsible for coordinating the plan, monitoring audits, updating statements, handling user requests and giving an accessibility opinion before any new service goes live.” Comment: stating the share of working time avoids a purely nominal lead. The RGAA asks for their functional position and duties; a lead with no access to project committees cannot influence decisions.

4. Human and financial resources

Sample text: “For the 2027-2029 period, [organisation] allocates [number] internal full-time equivalents and an annual budget of [amount] euros to digital accessibility, divided between audits, fixes, training and tools.” Comment: this is the heading most often left empty. An overall figure, even an approximate one, is better than none. If fixes are funded from project budgets, say so and explain how they are identified.

5. Skills, recruitment and training

Sample text: “Job descriptions for [development, design, web writing, purchasing] roles mention knowledge of digital accessibility rules. A training path is offered to [audiences], according to the timetable set out in the annual action plan.” Comment: this is where you meet the continuing training obligation in article 7 of the 2019 decree. The path is built role by role; our digital accessibility training courses are organised in this way, from content writers to developers.

6. Internal organisation and handling of requests

Sample text: “Every new service undergoes an accessibility check before going live. User requests received at [address or form] are handled by [department] within [time limit]. Each request receives a reply, a workaround where necessary and, where appropriate, an action included in the annual plan.” Comment: a written response time commits the organisation, and that is desirable; keep a register so that you can report on it in the review.

7. Purchasing, contracts and acceptance testing

Sample text: “Contracts and quotes for digital services include requirements for compliance with the RGAA, an award criterion relating to accessibility and an acceptance procedure. Agreements with partners who publish content on behalf of [organisation] include an accessibility clause.” Comment: the check on delivery is what gives the clause its effect; independent accessibility acceptance testing avoids discovering the defects at the first audit, once the supplier has been paid. Model clauses for each tender document, a scoring grid and penalties are set out in our article on digital accessibility clauses in public procurement.

8. Compliance work

Sample text: “Services will be assessed according to the following timetable: [table]. Fixes will give priority to the most visited content and to essential procedures: [list]. New projects include testing with disabled people for [type of project].” Comment: the RGAA expressly asks for disabled people to be included in user testing; state which projects will benefit, rather than making a general promise. A user test with disabled people on one key journey is enough to make this heading concrete.

9. Non-mandatory measures and review

Sample text: “Beyond its obligations, [organisation] plans [videos in sign language, a plain-language version of the most visited pages]. The review of the annual action plans is published each year together with the following plan.” Comment: non-mandatory measures add value to the approach, but they never replace fixing non-compliances. The review, missing from most plans in their second year, is nonetheless a heading expressly required by the RGAA.

The annual action plan: format, prioritisation and an example

The annual action plan turns the multi-year plan into dated tasks. The RGAA does not impose a format; an HTML table published on the accessibility page is both the easiest for users to read and the simplest to keep up to date. Avoid a scanned PDF or a spreadsheet to download: the plan itself must be published in an accessible format.

To prioritise, three criteria are enough in most cases: how serious the defect is for the user (a blocking defect prevents a procedure from being completed, a minor one slows it down), the audience of the service or journey, and the effort required to fix it. A blocking defect on a heavily used payment form comes before a hundred minor defects on archive pages. Defects in a shared component (a menu, a button, a form field in the design system) should be dealt with early, because a single fix benefits every page.

Extract from an annual digital accessibility action plan (fictitious example)
ActionServicePriorityOwnerDeadlineCompletion indicator
Full RGAA auditOnline procedures portal1Accessibility leadMarchReport delivered, statement updated
Fix the drop-down menu that cannot be used with a keyboardUser account area1Product teamAprilCriterion 7.3 passed at the follow-up audit
Replace PDF forms with online formsCorporate website1Communications departmentJuneNumber of forms migrated
Accessibility clause in the redesign contractIntranet2Purchasing departmentMayClause and award criterion included
Training for web content writersAll websites2Human resourcesSeptemberNumber of staff trained
Testing with blind and partially sighted usersAppointment booking2Project managerOctoberReport and corrective actions
Update statements and publish the next planAll services1Accessibility leadDecemberNext year’s plan online on 1 January

Wherever possible, each action refers to the number of the RGAA criterion concerned: that is what links it to the audit reports and to the list of non-compliances in the statement. The most frequent defects, such as insufficient contrast, poorly labelled forms or components that cannot be used with a keyboard, and the criteria added by WCAG 2.2, deserve a line of their own as soon as they affect a key journey.

Owners should be named by role rather than by person, so that the plan survives staff changes. In a group where development is outsourced or centralised abroad, the owner of an action can still sit in France, as the person responsible for obtaining the fix from the supplier or the central team; what matters is that someone answerable to the French entity is accountable for each line.

Budget and resources: costing the plan without making things up

The RGAA asks organisations to state the human and financial resources allocated to accessibility. There is no official scale, and no figure can be transposed from one organisation to another. A serious estimate starts from the inventory: number of services, frequency of audits, known volume of fixes, number of people to train and the lead’s share of working time.

  • Audits: the cost depends on the number of pages in the sample, the complexity of the components, the number of platforms (web, iOS, Android) and the follow-up audits planned; the factors that make a quote vary are detailed in our article on the price of an accessibility audit;
  • fixes: to be estimated with the development teams on the basis of the audit reports, distinguishing between fixes to shared components, which are few in number but structural, and page-by-page fixes;
  • content: production of accessible documents, subtitling, transcription and audio description of videos, rewriting of the most visited pages;
  • training: number of people per role and length of the learning paths;
  • internal time: the lead, project managers, writers and buyers, often forgotten even though it accounts for a large share of the effort.

Funding is available for public employers. In November 2023, the FIPHFP (the French fund for the integration of disabled people in the public service) and DINUM (Direction interministérielle du numérique, the French government’s interministerial digital directorate) renewed an agreement worth €20 million over four years (in French), which provides in particular for calls for projects aimed at local authorities. In its observations published on 18 June 2026, the Cour des comptes, France’s national audit office, notes that only 50% of the available FIPHFP funds had been committed, that the FIPHFP funds audits and recommendations rather than the compliance work itself, in the form of co-financing, and that the DINUM funding window, which can finance up to 100% of costs, is not open to local authorities. Mentioning in the plan the funding applied for shows that the budget has been thought through.

These public funds are not available to private companies. For a company subject to article 47, the budget question is usually one of allocation within the group: whether the French entity bears the cost of fixes to services built centrally, or whether they are charged to a group programme. Either answer is acceptable, as long as the plan states it.

Key point

A multi-year plan with no costed resources at all is the most visible sign of a window-dressing document. State at least the lead’s share of working time, the number of audits planned per year and an annual budget, even an approximate one, for fixes and training.

Indicators that make it possible to track the plan properly

The annual review required by the RGAA is only meaningful if it relies on indicators defined when the plan is adopted. The compliance rate is the best known, but it is not enough: a service can gain ten points by fixing minor defects while keeping a blocking defect at the payment step. Combine outcome indicators with input indicators.

Monitoring indicators for a multi-year digital accessibility plan
IndicatorTypeCalculationWhat it reveals
Share of services with a statement based on an audit less than three years oldOutcomeServices covered / services in the inventoryActual coverage of the obligation
RGAA compliance rate per serviceOutcomeOfficial RGAA method, on a constant scopeTechnical progress, service by service
Number of essential journeys with no blocking defectOutcomeJourneys tested end to end with no blocking defectWhat users actually experience
Average response time to user reportsOutcomeRegister of requestsQuality of the contact channel
Share of digital contracts with an accessibility clause and acceptance testingInputContracts awarded during the yearPrevention of future defects
Number of people trained per roleInputTraining planGrowth of in-house skills
Completion rate of the annual planInputActions completed / actions plannedReliability of the planning

For a public body, the Cour des comptes has highlighted the importance of end-to-end accessibility: in January 2026, only 7% of the main online public procedures complied with the 106 RGAA requirements, according to its observations published on 18 June 2026 (in French). The indicator of essential journeys with no blocking defect answers this concern directly: it requires looking at the whole procedure, from the home page to the confirmation, including modules bought from software vendors.

For a company, the same logic applies to the customer journeys that matter commercially: account creation, checkout, contract signature, claims. Reporting these indicators to the same governance body that approved the plan, once a year at least, is what keeps the document alive between two revisions.

The errors that lead to a breach, and how to avoid them

The errors below combine the failings expressly identified by Arcom with those that follow directly from the text of the law and from the RGAA. Almost all of them can be fixed in a few days, provided they are spotted before an inspection.

  1. Leaving last year’s plan online. This is the failing identified on impots.gouv.fr. Schedule publication of the following year’s plan for December, and check the link on 2 January.
  2. Publishing a plan longer than three years, or with no dates. The law limits the duration to three years. A “2021-2025 plan”, or a plan with no stated period, does not meet the requirement.
  3. Forgetting the link in the statement. Article 6 of the 2019 decree requires a link to the multi-year plan in every statement; the RGAA also requires a link to the plan for the current year.
  4. Making the plan hard to find. Article 47(IV) requires easy and direct access from the accessibility page. A document hidden in a “Publications” section is not enough.
  5. Publishing an inaccessible PDF. The multi-year plan and the action plan must be published in an accessible format. An image-only or untagged PDF contradicts the document it contains; an HTML page is preferable.
  6. Limiting the scope to the main websites. The plan covers all online public communication services: intranets, extranets, apps and software packages included.
  7. Leaving out the review. From the second year onwards, the RGAA expects a review of the annual plans. A plan that never says what has been done loses all credibility.
  8. Contradicting the statements. Announcing in the plan that every service has been audited, while several statements say that no audit has been carried out, invites an unfavourable cross-reading.
  9. Reducing the policy to non-mandatory measures. Sign language videos do not make up for a contact form that cannot be used with a keyboard.

A cross-reading of the three documents by someone outside the project, or an audit of documentary and technical compliance, makes it possible to spot these inconsistencies before a sworn inspector does. It is also the right moment to check that the accessibility page itself complies with the RGAA.

Local authority, public institution, large company: adapting the plan

Municipality, département, inter-municipal body

A local authority publishes a large number of documents (council decisions, by-laws, newsletters, forms) and buys most of its online services: school canteen payments, registrations, appointment booking, family portal. Its plan therefore needs to put the emphasis on purchasing, acceptance testing and document production. Having the plan approved by the executive, or even by a council decision, is not required by the texts but makes it easier for departments to apply it. Our page on the public sector explains how to build accessibility into procurement.

Public institution, university, hospital

These organisations often have dozens of websites for departments or laboratories, as well as e-learning platforms. The first task is the inventory, then rationalisation: closing or merging little-used websites is a legitimate accessibility measure, provided it is included in the plan. Teaching resources and online modules follow the same logic as other services.

Company with a turnover above €250 million

For a large company, the multi-year plan is one of the documents that Arcom’s power to impose penalties applies to directly. It must cover brand websites, customer areas, apps and employee tools published online. Within a group, each company that exceeds the threshold publishes its own plan, or a group plan that clearly identifies the companies and services covered. The plan is also an opportunity to organise, with the same resources, the compliance of journeys subject to the EAA: our page for large organisations presents this twofold approach.

Foreign group with a French subsidiary above the threshold

A group headquartered in Luxembourg, Belgium, Switzerland or elsewhere is not subject to article 47 as such; its French subsidiaries are, one by one. Since the threshold is calculated for each legal person on the average turnover generated in France over the last three closed financial years, a group may have one French company that is covered and another that is not. The first step is therefore a list of French entities with their turnover, checked each year, because a subsidiary can cross the threshold after an acquisition or a merger.

Once the covered entities are known, the group has to choose between separate plans per subsidiary and a single group plan. A single plan is easier to maintain when the same teams build the services, but it must name each covered company, list its services and identify its accessibility lead, so that an inspector can see at once which commitments apply to which entity. Whatever the choice, each covered service still needs its own French-format statement linking to the plan and to the current action plan, and the plan must be accessible from each of those services.

Two pitfalls recur in international groups. The first is publishing a group accessibility policy, written in English for several countries, and assuming it fulfils the French obligation: it rarely contains the RGAA headings, a three-year period or a dated annual plan. The second is leaving the plan with a central team that does not track French deadlines, so that the action plan is not renewed on 1 January. Appointing a lead within the French entity, even if most of the work is done centrally, addresses both.

RGAA 5: should you rewrite your multi-year plan?

DINUM has announced the publication of RGAA 5 at the end of 2026 (in French). As of 12 November 2026, the official website still shows version 4.1.2 and states that version 5 is being drafted. According to the announcement, the future framework incorporates WCAG 2.2, and statements published before its release will remain valid for eighteen months, within a limit of three years from their publication. The announcement does not mention any change to the obligations relating to the multi-year plan or the annual plan.

There is therefore no reason to wait for RGAA 5 before adopting or renewing a plan. The right approach is to include in the 2027-2029 plan an explicit migration action: training teams in the new criteria, updating acceptance grids and contract clauses, and scheduling re-audits of services under the new version, starting with those whose statement is about to expire. DINUM also states that work based on RGAA 4.1.2 should not be suspended while awaiting the new version. Our article on digital accessibility standards places the RGAA in relation to WCAG and the EN 301 549 standard.

Publishing a compliant multi-year accessibility plan in 90 days: the action plan

For an organisation that has no multi-year plan, or whose plan has expired, here is a realistic sequence. It assumes an appointed project lead and a decision by senior management on resources halfway through.

  1. Days 1 to 10: appoint the lead and check what exists. Appoint the accessibility lead, list the documents online (statements, previous plan, action plans) and immediately fix the most visible failings: a plan for a past year, a broken link, an incorrect compliance status.
  2. Days 10 to 40: carry out the initial assessment. Inventory of services, audits and statements, contracts, skills and user reports, using the method described above.
  3. Days 40 to 55: cost and decide. Present senior management with a timetable for audits and fixes, a training plan and an annual budget. This is the step that turns the document into a commitment.
  4. Days 55 to 70: write the multi-year plan and the first annual plan. Follow the order of the RGAA headings, attach the list of services as an appendix and date every action in the plan.
  5. Days 70 to 80: obtain approval. Have the plan adopted by the competent body and record the date of approval in the preamble.
  6. Days 80 to 90: publish and link. Put the multi-year plan and the action plan online in HTML on the accessibility page, add the links to every statement, check direct access from the footer and schedule publication of next year’s plan now.

This timetable is compatible with the two-month deadline that Arcom granted, in its June 2026 decision, for the documentary obligations: the first actions, those of the first ten days, are enough to remove the failings that are easiest to establish, while the substantive work continues. The page on digital accessibility in France summarises the other obligations to address in parallel.

Frequently asked questions

What is a SPAN in digital accessibility?

SPAN is the common French abbreviation for schéma pluriannuel d’accessibilité numérique, called in the law the schéma pluriannuel de mise en accessibilité, or multi-year accessibility plan. Required by article 47(III) of the French law of 11 February 2005, it sets out, for a maximum of three years, the organisation’s accessibility policy, its resources, its organisation and the timetable for audits and fixes. It is made public and broken down each year into an action plan.

Is the multi-year accessibility plan mandatory for a private company?

Yes, for companies subject to article 47, that is, those whose turnover generated in France exceeds €250 million, and for private bodies entrusted with a public service mission. For these companies, Arcom can penalise a missing or non-compliant multi-year plan and action plan, with a fine of up to €25,000 after a formal notice that has gone unheeded. Companies subject only to the EAA do not have this obligation.

What is the maximum duration of a multi-year accessibility plan?

Three years. The law states that the duration of the plan may not exceed three years. Nothing prevents an organisation from choosing a shorter period or revising it before it ends, for example after a major redesign or the release of a new framework. An expired plan must be replaced without delay, and the action plan for the current year must be published every year.

Where should the multi-year plan and the action plan be published?

On the organisation’s website, in an accessible format, preferably in HTML on the accessibility page. The law requires easy and direct access to the multi-year plan and to the plan for the current year, and the accessibility statement of each service must contain a link to them. Plans for previous years may remain online in a separate archive section.

Is one multi-year plan enough for several websites?

Yes. The plan covers all of the organisation’s online public communication services: a single document covers all its websites, intranets, extranets, apps and software packages. Each service, however, keeps its own accessibility statement, based on its own audit, and each statement refers to the same plan. Attach the list of services covered as an appendix so that the scope can be checked.

What is the risk if the action plan is not up to date?

An action plan covering a past year is a breach of article 47(IV): this is what Arcom found in June 2026 regarding impots.gouv.fr, with two months to remedy it. If the formal notice goes unheeded, a financial penalty of up to €25,000 may be imposed, and imposed again if the failing persists six months later.

Should we wait for RGAA 5 before writing our plan?

No. RGAA 5 is announced for the end of 2026, and the official announcement does not change the obligations relating to the multi-year plan and the annual plan. DINUM asks organisations not to suspend work based on RGAA 4.1.2. Simply include a migration action in the plan: training in the new criteria, updated acceptance grids and a re-audit timetable.
